title: Museum family workshops
brief:
Prepare a decision paper for a local museum education committee selecting four family workshops. Fictional history from two events per format gives seats offered, registrations, attendees, completed surveys, respondents likely to return, and supply spending. Printmaking: 48, 46, 38, 32, 25, $224. Story objects: 60, 47, 41, 35, 24, $110. Paper architecture: 48, 48, 42, 25, 22, $180. Family gallery games: 64, 54, 50, 40, 28, $86. All events require equal staff time. Include at least one making workshop and one gallery-based workshop, and cap supplies at $340. Compare participation and survey results, recommend a lineup, and explain how uneven survey response affects your confidence.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

984cc0f281896fb9.text:
# Decision paper for the museum education committee

**Approve one paper architecture workshop and three family gallery games workshops.** This gives families one opportunity to make something and three opportunities to explore the galleries through play. Using half of each format’s two-event supply spending as the estimate for one workshop, the lineup would cost **$219**, leaving **$121** of the $340 supply budget available. At historical attendance averages, it would provide 192 family workshop visits across 216 offered seats. Those are individual attendances, so a family member who comes twice contributes two visits.

The recommendation gives priority to participation. With four dates and equal staff time per event, the committee’s principal choice is how to use each date. Gallery games reached the most people per event, while paper architecture attracted the most attendees of the two clearly identified making formats. The strongest reason to choose a different lineup would be to give families a second chance to attend a making workshop. That is a meaningful tradeoff, and the historical figures put a price on it.

## What the participation record shows

Each row below combines two events. The registration rate measures how much of the offered capacity families booked. The show-up rate measures how many registrants attended. Attendance per event is the most direct measure of how many people the museum reached with one date on its calendar.

| Format | Seats offered | Registrations | Attendees | Seats booked | Registrants attending | Attendees per event | Supplies per event |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Printmaking | 48 | 46 | 38 | 95.8% | 82.6% | 19 | $112 |
| Story objects | 60 | 47 | 41 | 78.3% | 87.2% | 20.5 | $55 |
| Paper architecture | 48 | 48 | 42 | 100.0% | 87.5% | 21 | $90 |
| Family gallery games | 64 | 54 | 50 | 84.4% | 92.6% | 25 | $43 |

Paper architecture and printmaking offer the cleanest comparison. Both offered 24 seats per event. Paper architecture filled its registration lists and averaged 21 attendees. Printmaking came close to filling its lists and averaged 19 attendees. Choosing paper architecture for the making date would therefore reach two more people at historical averages and save $22 in supplies. Full registration suggests that scheduling the making date at a time families can attend matters. Without a waitlist count, however, the committee cannot tell how many additional people would have booked.

Gallery games illustrate why the percentage of seats booked can give a different impression from the head count. The format left ten places unbooked across two events, yet its larger capacity and strong follow-through produced 50 attendees. Only four of its 54 registrants missed the event. For a committee trying to reach families with a fixed number of dates, the consequential figure is 25 people attending per use of staff time. The format also had the lowest supply spending, at $43 per event, or $1.72 per attendee over the two events.

Story objects merits consideration despite having the lowest booking rate. Its two events drew 41 attendees, just one fewer than paper architecture, and cost $70 less in total. It offers the committee a relatively inexpensive way to broaden the subject matter of the series. Its participation record gives less support for using it in place of a gallery games date, where the historical difference is 4.5 visits per event.

## What families said about returning

| Format | Completed surveys | Survey response among attendees | Respondents likely to return | Likely to return among respondents | Confirmed likely-to-return responses per 100 attendees |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Printmaking | 32 | 84.2% | 25 | 78.1% | 65.8 |
| Story objects | 35 | 85.4% | 24 | 68.6% | 58.5 |
| Paper architecture | 25 | 59.5% | 22 | 88.0% | 52.4 |
| Family gallery games | 40 | 80.0% | 28 | 70.0% | 56.0 |

Paper architecture drew the most favorable responses among families who completed a survey. Twenty-two of its 25 respondents said they were likely to return. Printmaking also received favorable responses, with 25 of 32 respondents likely to return. Gallery games and story objects had similar rates, at 70.0% and 68.6%. With just two events per format, a difference that small offers little basis for choosing between them. Gallery games nevertheless produced the largest *number* of likely-to-return responses, 28, because it reached more people and collected more surveys.

Uneven response matters most to the choice of making workshop. Paper architecture’s headline figure of 88.0% leaves the views of 17 of its 42 attendees unknown. Printmaking missed only six of its 38 attendees. Counting the affirmative responses against everyone who attended changes the ranking. Printmaking obtained a likely-to-return response from 65.8% of all attendees, while paper architecture obtained one from 52.4%. This second measure tells the committee how much favorable intent each format actually documented. An attendee who skipped the survey could still be eager to return.

The missing responses leave room for materially different conclusions. If none of paper architecture’s 17 nonrespondents were likely to return, the share among all attendees would be 52.4%. If all 17 were likely to return, it would be 92.9%. The corresponding range for printmaking is 65.8% to 81.6%. These are the limits allowed by the missing answers. There is no evidence about where within them the true shares fall. The committee can be confident that many respondents enjoyed enough of the experience to express interest in another visit. It has much less reason to conclude that paper architecture generates the strongest intention to return across its whole audience. Actual repeat attendance remains unmeasured for every format.

## The choice across four dates

The following options all include a making workshop and gallery games. The estimates assume each date repeats its format’s historical average for attendance and supplies. Fractional visits reflect averaging across past events.

| Four-workshop lineup | Estimated visits | Estimated supplies | Budget remaining |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| One paper architecture, three gallery games | 96 | $219 | $121 |
| Two paper architecture, two gallery games | 92 | $266 | $74 |
| One paper architecture, one story objects, two gallery games | 91.5 | $231 | $109 |
| One of each format | 85.5 | $300 | $40 |

**The recommended lineup provides 96 estimated visits across 120 offered seats.** The four-date calculation is 21 attendees for paper architecture plus 25 for each of three gallery games dates. This corrects the opening participation estimate, which used the two-event totals instead of the per-event figures. Supply spending is $90 for the making date and $129 for the three gallery dates.

A second paper architecture date is the closest alternative. For an additional $47 in supplies and an estimated four fewer visits, it would offer 24 more making seats and a second date for families who cannot come to the first. If the committee values access to making on two different dates more highly than four additional visits, that option fits comfortably under the cap. A series featuring all four formats would give families the widest choice and would also meet the budget. The historical cost of that breadth is 10.5 fewer visits and $81 more in supplies than the recommended lineup.

The largest uncertainty in the recommendation is demand for a third gallery games date. The record covers only two events, and the combined figures conceal whether turnout held steady or varied substantially between them. A useful threshold is 21 attendees. If the third gallery games date attracts fewer than 21, a second paper architecture date at its historical average would reach more people. The museum could schedule the making workshop early and record requests after it fills. That would give the committee direct evidence about unmet demand when it next considers the balance of gallery and making dates.

For this cycle, approve the $219 lineup on the strength of observed attendance and cost. At all four workshops, offer the same short return-intention question at the same point before departure and record attendance and survey completions separately for each date. That small change would let the next committee see whether the third gallery date sustained participation and whether paper architecture’s favorable survey result holds when more of its attendees answer.

# Decision paper for the museum education committee

## Recommendation

Schedule **one printmaking workshop, one paper architecture workshop, and two family gallery games workshops**. Estimated supply spending is **$288**, leaving **$52** under the $340 cap. Based on the historical per-event averages, the lineup would offer 112 seats, draw about 101 registrations, and generate about 90 attendances across four sessions.

This lineup gives families two distinct making activities and two opportunities to participate in a gallery-based workshop. Paper architecture had the strongest demand relative to capacity. Printmaking also came close to filling its registration places and had a high survey response rate. Family gallery games drew the largest audiences, converted the most registrations into attendance, and had the lowest supply cost. The recommendation gives those participation results more weight than small differences in reported likelihood of returning.

## Participation and supply costs

The historical figures combine two events per format. The table uses the combined counts to calculate rates and divides the supply spending by two to estimate the cost of a future session. Because all formats require equal staff time, each four-session lineup carries the same staffing commitment.

| Format | Seats offered | Registrations | Attendees | Seats registered | Seats attended | Registrants who attended | Supplies per event |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Printmaking | 48 | 46 | 38 | 95.8% | 79.2% | 82.6% | $112 |
| Story objects | 60 | 47 | 41 | 78.3% | 68.3% | 87.2% | $55 |
| Paper architecture | 48 | 48 | 42 | 100.0% | 87.5% | 87.5% | $90 |
| Family gallery games | 64 | 54 | 50 | 84.4% | 78.1% | 92.6% | $43 |

**Paper architecture** filled all 48 registration places and drew 42 attendees, giving it the highest attendance relative to seats offered. At an estimated $90 per session, it is the stronger choice for the first making slot on participation and cost. Its full registration establishes that the places offered were taken. The figures provide no count of families who may have tried to register after it filled.

**Printmaking** registered 46 people for 48 places. Eight registrants did not attend, giving it the lowest registration-to-attendance conversion of the four formats. It still filled about four in five available seats on the day. At $112 per session, printmaking is the most expensive option. The case for including it rests on strong registration demand and the opportunity to offer a second kind of making activity.

**Family gallery games** drew 50 attendees across two events, or 25 per session, the highest average in the comparison. Its larger seating capacity helped it reach that total, and 50 of its 54 registrants attended. It also had the lowest supply spending per attendee at $1.72, compared with $2.68 for story objects, $4.29 for paper architecture, and $5.89 for printmaking. A second gallery games session draws on the format’s combination of reach, reliable turnout among registrants, and low cost.

**Story objects** attracted 41 attendees across two events, three more than printmaking, and cost just $55 per session. It also had the lowest share of offered seats registered and the lowest share occupied on the day. It would be a reasonable choice if the committee’s priority were to represent all four formats. For this slate, the second gallery games session is projected to draw 4.5 more attendances than a story objects session while saving $12 in supplies.

## Survey results and confidence

| Format | Completed surveys | Share of attendees who responded | Respondents likely to return | Share of respondents likely to return |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Printmaking | 32 | 84.2% | 25 | 78.1% |
| Story objects | 35 | 85.4% | 24 | 68.6% |
| Paper architecture | 25 | 59.5% | 22 | 88.0% |
| Family gallery games | 40 | 80.0% | 28 | 70.0% |

Paper architecture had the highest stated likelihood of returning among respondents, at 22 of 25. It also had the lowest survey coverage. Seventeen of its 42 attendees did not complete a survey, compared with six each for printmaking and story objects and ten for gallery games. If willingness to complete the survey was related to the experience attendees had, the missing responses could shift the results in either direction. The figures do not establish why people skipped the survey.

The extent of that uncertainty can be illustrated by using all attendees as the denominator. For paper architecture, 22 of 42 attendees, or 52.4%, are recorded as likely to return. If all 17 attendees with missing surveys would also have answered positively, the figure would be 39 of 42, or 92.9%. The equivalent ranges are 65.8% to 81.6% for printmaking, 58.5% to 73.2% for story objects, and 56.0% to 76.0% for gallery games. These are the extremes allowed by the missing responses. They are neither forecasts nor statistical confidence intervals.

The ranges overlap, so a ranking of all attendees by likelihood of returning would depend on assumptions about the people who did not respond. Printmaking’s 25 positive responses cover almost two-thirds of all its attendees, giving the committee a firmer basis for treating its survey result as a sign of interest. Story objects and gallery games differ by just 1.4 percentage points among respondents, too small a gap to drive the selection. Gallery games also recorded the largest number of positive answers, at 28, although it had the largest audience and the most completed surveys. All four results measure stated intention at the time of the survey. The history does not track whether respondents subsequently returned.

For the committee’s decision, paper architecture earns its place through full registration and strong attendance. The survey adds an encouraging signal from those who responded, with limited confidence about the wider audience. Printmaking has stronger survey coverage, and the case for repeating gallery games comes primarily from observed participation.

## Lineup trade-offs

| Four-session lineup | Estimated supplies | Expected attendances |
|---|---:|---:|
| **One printmaking, one paper architecture, two gallery games** | **$288** | **90** |
| One of each format | $300 | 85.5 |
| Two paper architecture, two gallery games | $266 | 92 |
| One paper architecture, three gallery games | $219 | 96 |

The alternatives show what the committee gains and gives up through the choice of formats. Offering one of each gives story objects a place and provides the broadest range of activities. Repeating paper architecture instead of including printmaking saves $22 and projects two additional attendances. Running three gallery games sessions and one paper architecture session gives the highest projected attendance and the lowest spending among the options shown, with a single making session. The recommended lineup gives up those projected gains to retain two different making experiences while still offering the gallery activity twice.

These estimates assume that each future session performs like the average of its two historical events and that repeating a format does not materially change demand for it. The combined figures do not show how much turnout or cost varied between individual events. Projected attendances count visits across sessions, so the same family could contribute to more than one session total. The $52 margin leaves room for supply costs to vary, and actual orders should fit within the $340 cap.

Approve **one printmaking session, one paper architecture session, and two family gallery games sessions**. If maximizing projected attendance becomes the committee’s overriding priority, the three-games lineup is the strongest option in the comparison. For a program that values both reach and variety in hands-on making, the recommended lineup offers two distinct making activities alongside the format with the strongest observed turnout.
